      50             : /// A class to encapsulate construction axes of an Tensor.  TensorOptions was
      51             : /// designed to support the Python style API for specifying construction options
      52             : /// on factory functions, e.g.,
      53             : ///
      54             : ///     torch.zeros(2, 3, dtype=torch.int32)
      55             : ///
      56             : /// Because C++ doesn't natively support keyword arguments, there must be
      57             : /// another way of specifying keyword-like arguments.  TensorOptions is a
      58             : /// builder class which can be used to construct this "dictionary" of keyword
      59             : /// arguments: functions which support TensorOptions conventionally take this
      60             : /// argument optionally as their last argument.
      61             : ///
      62             : /// WARNING: In PyTorch, there are `torch::` variants of factory functions,
      63             : /// e.g., torch::zeros for at::zeros.  These return Variables (while the
      64             : /// stock ATen functions return plain Tensors).  If you mix these functions
      65             : /// up, you WILL BE SAD.
      66             : ///
      67             : /// Rather than use the constructor of this class directly, you should prefer to
      68             : /// use the constructor functions, and then chain setter methods on top of them.
      69             : ///
      70             : ///     at::device(at::kCUDA).dtype(kInt)
      71             : ///     at::dtype(at::kInt)
      72             : ///
      73             : /// Additionally, anywhere a TensorOptions is expected, you can directly
      74             : /// pass at::kCUDA / at::kInt, and it will implicitly convert to a
      75             : /// TensorOptions.
      76             : ///
      77             : /// Here are some recommended ways to create a 2x2 tensor of zeros
      78             : /// with certain properties.  These all *implicitly* make use of
      79             : /// TensorOptions, even if they don't mention the class explicitly:
      80             : ///
      81             : ///     at::zeros({2,2}, at::kCUDA);
      82             : ///     at::zeros({2,2}, at::kLong);
      83             : ///     at::zeros({2,2}, at::device(at::kCUDA).dtype(at::kLong()));
      84             : ///     at::zeros({2,2}, at::device({at::kCUDA, 1})); // place on device 1
      85             : ///     at::zeros({2,2}, at::requires_grad());

      88             : /// NOTE [ TensorOptions Constructors ]
      89             : ///
      90             : /// TensorOptions is like a dictionary with entries from the set:
      91             : /// {requires_grad, device, dtype, layout}, where each entry may be
      92             : /// unspecified (i.e., is optional). It is used to specify the properties of
      93             : /// tensors in many places both in C++ internal and API, e.g., tensor factory
      94             : /// methods like `at::empty({10}, options)`, tensor conversions like
      95             : /// `tensor.to(...)`, etc.
      96             : ///
      97             : /// To provide a simple API that is consistent with Python, where one can do
      98             : /// `torch.empty(sizes, X)` with `X` being a `torch.device`, `torch.dtype`, or a
      99             : /// `torch.layout`, we want TensorOptions to be implicitly convertible from
     100             : /// `ScalarType dtype`, `Layout layout` and `Device device`. Therefore, we have
     101             : /// three implicit constructors from each of these three types.
     102             : ///
     103             : /// This is sufficient for `ScalarType` and `Layout` as they are simple Enum
     104             : /// classes. However, `Device` is an ordinary class with implicit constructors
     105             : /// `Device(DeviceType, DeviceIndex = -1)` and `Device(std::string)` to be
     106             : /// consistent with Python API, where strings are treated as equivalent with a
     107             : /// `torch.device` object (e.g., "cuda:1" can be passed to everywhere a
     108             : /// `torch.device("cuda:1")` is accepted). To support the syntax
     109             : /// `at::empty({10}, {kCUDA, 1})` and `tensor.to(kCUDA)`, we need to make sure
     110             : /// that `TensorOptions` is implicitly constructible with any arguments that a
     111             : /// `Device` can constructed from. So we have,
     112             : ///
     113             : ///    /* implicit */ TensorOptions(T&& device) : TensorOptions() {
     114             : ///      this->set_device(device);
     115             : ///    }
     116             : ///
     117             : ///    template <typename... Args,
     118             : ///             typename = std::enable_if_t<std::is_constructible<Device,
     119             : ///             Args&&...>::value>>
     120             : ///    /* implicit */  TensorOptions(Args&&... args)
     121             : ///     : TensorOptions(Device(std::forward<Args>(args)...)) {}
     122             : ///
     123             : ///
     124             : /// But this will be problematic. Consider this: `TensorOptions({kCUDA, 1})`.
     125             : /// Compiler will complain about ambiguity between the copy constructor and the
     126             : /// `Device` constructor because `{kCUDA, 1}` can be converted to both a
     127             : /// `TensorOption` and a `Device`.
     128             : ///
     129             : /// To get around this, we templatize the `Device` constructor. Since overload
     130             : /// resolution is done before template resolution, our problem is solved.
